20863-major-vigoureux:
Sergeant Archelaus digs in a neglected garden as Major Vigoureux opens in talk of trousers. The Commandant's sharp query halts the long man mid-spade. He grounds his spade like a musket and stands to face the charge.

Arthur Quiller-Couch sets this tale of 1907 among the Scilly Isles' small garrison. An ageing major, a dull post, and a sudden call to act drive the plot. Q, as readers called him, blends humour with a seaman's love of Cornwall's coasts. The book charms with its gentle pace before duty turns the quiet post upside down.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-cite:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Cîteaux describes the mother house of the Cistercian Order. St. Robert, Abbot of Molesme, founded it in 1098. Robert and twenty companions settled a deserted, marshy place in the diocese of Châlons, where rushes called cistels gave the site its name.

There they began the literal observance of St. Benedict's Rule, in a new monastery distinguished from Molesme, on land given by Raynald, Viscount of Beaune, and his wife Hodierna. The name Cîteaux soon replaced Novum Monasterium, and the order that grew from this marshy valley spread across Europe. The entry traces the foundation, its patrons and the beginnings of Cistercian life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-clai:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Clairvaux describes the third daughter of Cîteaux. St. Bernard founded it in 1115 in a deep Aube valley, then called the Valley of Wormwood. Hughes the First, Count of Troyes, gave the valley to the Cistercian colony. By a charter of 1116 the house is already called Clara Vallis, or Clairvaux.

After a trying beginning, Clairvaux grew rapidly under Bernard, whose renown drew so many postulants that in his lifetime it planted sixty-eight daughter houses. Those houses stood across France, Italy, Germany, England, Spain and Portugal. Colonies went to Trois-Fontaines in 1116 and to Fontenay in 1119. The entry follows Clairvaux's astonishing expansion under its great abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnulf-of-lis: A 1913 entry on Arnulf of Lisieux — the bishop and statesman. Thomas Shahan honors his letters. He served Henry II's troubled reign. The schools prized his Latin. A prelate of the Angevin court. His see guarded the Norman coast. His letters survive in the collections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bayeux: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Bayeux — the Norman diocese of the tapestry town. Georges Goyau gives its story. Its cathedral crowns the old streets. The embroidery tells the Conquest's tale. A see of the Calvados. Its lace is famed through France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benoit-marie-: A 1913 entry on Cardinal Langénieux — the Archbishop of Reims. Joseph Sollier honors his long rule. He crowned the Third Republic's peace. The champagne city knew his zeal. A prince of the French Church. His red hat crowned long service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bordeaux: A 1913 entry on Bordeaux — the Aquitanian archdiocese. Georges Goyau gives its wine-country story. Its primates rule the southwest. St. André crowns the old town. A see of the Gironde's banks. Its vineyards are famed through the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-batte: A 1913 entry on Charles Batteux — the aesthetician of the fine arts. Gerhard Gietmann notes his famous treatise. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the Paris schools. A writer of the eighteenth century. His Beaux-Arts is the aestheticians' text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crusade-of-th: This 1913 reference article on the Crusade of the Pastoureaux — the shepherds' rising. Louis Bréhier unfolds its tragic tale. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evreux: A 1913 entry on Évreux — the Norman diocese. Georges Goyau gives its ancient story. Its bishops date from the early age. The Iton guards the old town. A see of the Norman valley. Its 1077 cathedral is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-of-c: A 1913 entry on Geoffrey of Clairvaux — the abbot-biographer. Francis Schaefer honors his famous Vita. His pen enshrined the holy Bernard. The order prized its learned son. The Boswell of the mellifluous doctor. His 1188 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-buteu: This 1913 reference article on Buteux — the Jesuit martyr. Edward Spillane honors his blessed death. He died for the Canadian missions. The faithful keep his memory. A martyr among the North American saints. His 1652 martyrdom is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-devereux: This 1913 reference piece on Devereux — an Irish writer of note. Thomas Kernan lists his works. Little is known of his career. The nineteenth century was his period. The Dublin press knew his pen. His 1890 works are famed. His 1890 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-marcou: This 1913 reference piece on Marcoux — the Canadian missionary. Florence McGahan recounts his mission years. His zeal served the northern flock. The Church prized its fearless son. The missions bless his name. His 1855 death is famed. His 1855 missions are famed. His 1855 northern missions are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laurence-vaux: A 1913 entry on Vaux — an English writer of note. Vincent Scully surveys his works. Little survives about his life. The sixteenth century was his time. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-loucheux: This 1913 reference piece on the Loucheux — the Yukon tribes. Adrian Morice unfolds their mission tale. The Oblates braved the northern wilds. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-meaux: A 1913 entry on Meaux — the Brie diocese. Georges Goyau gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Marne flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the French north. Its 4th-century see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-levad: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Levadoux — an American priest of note. Arthur Jones sketches his parish years. Few details of his life remain. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-deve: This biographical entry profiles Nicholas Devereux, an American Catholic philanthropist of the 1800s, tracing his career, his charities, and his standing as the 1913 editors understood it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's American gallery, preserved among its records of Catholic philanthropists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-boile: Boileau was the lawgiver of French classicism, whose Art poétique taught poets the rules of reason and clarity. This entry covers his satires, his criticism, and his enormous authority. The legislator of Parnassus: his satires spared neither bad poets nor bad morals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-letou: This biographical entry profiles Nicolas Letourneux, a French priest and moralist of the 1600s, tracing his career, his devotional writings, and his place among the spiritual writers of his age as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's French gallery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perigueux: Périgueux, the city of the Dordogne, became a diocese with a Romanesque cathedral. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The Church in the land of truffles and towers: its great domed St-Front is a Byzantine jewel of France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-therese: St. Thérèse of Lisieux was the Little Flower. This long entry examines her life, her way, and her fame. The Carmelite of the little way: her little story conquered the world in 1898's pages of the Carmel in Lisieux's Normandy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sigebert-of-g: Sigebert of Gembloux was the chronicler of the abbey. This entry examines his chronicle, his learning, and his fame. The annalist of the Lotharingian monks: his learned chronicle filled Gembloux in the 1100s' abbey in the cloister of the monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-caryll-mo: Sir Caryll Molyneux, the English Catholic of the penal age, held the Sefton title. This brief entry notes his life and his constancy. A quiet name from the recusants: his brave constancy crowned Sefton in the 1700s' Lancashire in the hall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bernard-of: St. Bernard of Clairvaux was the mellifluous doctor. This very long entry examines his Cistercians, his crusade, and his fame. The last father of the Church: his honeyed voice filled Clairvaux in the 1130s' Burgundy in the abbey of the valley.
myths-and-legends-of-the-sioux:
Marie L. McLaughlin dedicates these Sioux tales to her mother's memory. Most stories here were told to her at her mother's knee. The contents open with the Forgotten Ear of Corn. The Little Mice and the Pet Rabbit follow.

Rabbit tales run through the book, meeting elk, bears, and grouse girls. The Legend of Standing Rock and the Peace Pipe story anchor the set. Unktomi the trickster loses his tail in one tale. Faithful lovers, lost wives, and a lone warrior fill out the list. McLaughlin, of Sioux heritage herself, saved oral tales in print for new generations.
phineas-redux: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Phineas Redux, an editorial note and the start of the contents, with no chapter text visible. The note records that Anthony Trollope's novel ran in the Graphic from July 1873 to January 1874. It appeared in book form from Chapman and Hall in 1874, with illustrations by Frank Holl. The contents open with Temptation, Harrington Hall, and Phineas among his old friends, returning the Irish member to Parliament.
the-ball-at-sceaux:
Honore de Balzac's tale, translated by Clara Bell, centres on the Comte de Fontaine, head of an old Poitou family. Fontaine served the Bourbon cause in the Vendee war and was left for dead at Les Quatre Chemins. Ruined by confiscation, he refused posts offered by Napoleon.

Faithful to his class, he married a penniless woman from an old Breton family rather than a rich upstart's kin. In Paris with a large family, he receives rank and crosses he did not seek. Those favours shake his plan to return home and draw him toward a private audience with the king.
the-heritage-of-the-sioux:
B. M. Bower wrote The Heritage of the Sioux. The contents list twenty-one chapters, among them When Green Grass Comes, The Daughter of a Chief, Adventure Comes Smiling, The Wild-Goose Chase, and In the Devil's Frying-Pan. Chapter one rides with Old Applehead Furrman across the mesa from Albuquerque, sniffing a soft spring breeze.

Green grass in sheltered places means calves and roundup time. Applehead owns about a thousand head, yet age has made him content to hire trusted men for the big roundups and skip the hard work. This spring feels different, though. Some stir of ambition or feeling moves in him, and the wide spaces call as they did in his cowpuncher days.
the-phantom-of-the-opera-by-gaston-lerou: Gaston Leroux's The Phantom of the Opera is listed here with a 1909 date. The pages present hold a table of contents only, so the novel itself does not appear. The list names title and copyright pages, a section on the world of Gaston Leroux, and an introduction, then a prologue and chapters. Is It The Ghost?, The New Margarita, Box Five, and Apollo's Lyre appear, and the list ends at chapter fifteen, Christine! Christine! Three other records of the novel carry differing contents lists.
